I am working on high-resolution spectroscopy in the group of
Prof. Snellen
at Leiden Observatory.


 Research focus
High-resolution spectroscopy of exoplanets, brown dwarfs, and cool stars — composition, thermal structure, and isotope ratios as tracers of formation and chemical evolution.


About me

I am a PhD candidate at Leiden Observatory (2023–2027), interested in observational astronomy and exoplanet science. I enjoy developing tools for data reduction and analysis of high-resolution spectroscopy data. During my PhD, I have contributed to the ESO SupJup survey to disentangle the formation pathways of giant planets and brown dwarfs through isotopic ratios. I am also experienced in data reduction and analysis of JWST/NIRSpec observations of brown dwarfs. During my PhD, I have also extended our modelling efforts to fit the high-resolution spectra of M-dwarfs. Currently, I am working on both directly-imaged planets and M-dwarfs to push forward the understanding of their atmospheres and formation pathways.

title: Research

Research

My work combines high-resolution spectroscopy, atmospheric retrievals, and careful data reduction to study the chemistry of giant planets, brown dwarfs, and cool stars — with a particular focus on isotope ratios as tracers of formation and Galactic chemical evolution.

title: Data Reduction & Modelling
content: ← All research topics Data reduction & modelling Reliable atmospheric inference depends as much on how spectra are extracted and calibrated as on the forward model. Much of my work sits at that interface: building reductions for faint companions, validating detections of weak isotopologues, and coupling flexible radiative-transfer models to Bayesian samplers. Pipelines and extraction For VLT/CRIRES+ programmes I use and contribute to reductions based on excalibuhr (dark/flat correction, order tracing, nodding, wavelength calibration). For close-in companions (e.g. β Pic b), I developed a spectral-extraction scheme that co-adds spatial rows weighted by the planet’s cross-correlation strength after subtracting a jointly fitted stellar model — improving S/N when the target sits on a bright scattered-light background. Archival SPIRou spectra for M dwarfs were quality-filtered (S/N, airmass, seeing) and coadded with barycentric alignment, with uncertainties that capture epoch-to-epoch variance. Atmospheric retrievals My standard modelling stack combines: Line-by-line radiative transfer with petitRADTRANS and up-to-date molecular/atomic opacities. Flexible P–T profiles (piecewise gradients at selected pressure nodes) rather than fixed grids alone. Chemistry from FastChem equilibrium, with optional logarithmic abundance offsets per species when the data demand it. Nested sampling to map posteriors and compare models with/without rare isotopologues via Bayesian evidence — the same...

title: Exoplanet Atmospheres
content: ← All research topics Exoplanet atmospheres Young, self-luminous giant planets and brown dwarfs share temperatures, molecular inventories, and spectral morphologies. That makes young brown dwarfs excellent laboratories for the same physics that shapes directly imaged exoplanets, while companions such as β Pic b let us test formation tracers in a planetary-mass atmosphere. What this is about Atmospheric characterisation aims to recover the pressure–temperature structure, molecular abundances, metallicity, carbon-to-oxygen ratio (C/O), clouds, and — when the data allow — isotopic ratios. These quantities encode where and how an object formed: snow lines in the protoplanetary disc set the volatile inventory available for accretion, while subsequent evolution (clouds, mixing, irradiation) reshapes the emergent spectrum. My contribution I lead atmospheric retrieval analyses of high-resolution and JWST spectra of young substellar objects: β Pic b — From 11 nights of VLT/CRIRES+ K-band spectroscopy, combined with near-infrared photometry, I measured $^{12}\mathrm{C}/^{13}\mathrm{C}=58^{+18}{-15}$, with $T{\mathrm{eff}}\approx 1630\,\mathrm{K}$, near-solar metallicity, and a solar-like C/O (A&A 2026). Multi-epoch analysis was essential to fold night-to-night scatter into the uncertainties. GQ Lup B and its host — As part of the ESO SupJup Survey, I constrained the carbon isotope ratio of the companion and the star in the same system (A&A 2025)....

title: High-Resolution Spectroscopy
content: ← All research topics High-resolution spectroscopy Resolving individual molecular lines transforms atmospheric characterisation: line depths and shapes constrain abundances and temperature structure, while line positions encode radial and rotational velocities. For isotope work, resolving $^{12}\mathrm{CO}$ from $^{13}\mathrm{CO}$ (and oxygen isotopologues) is often only possible at high resolving power. Instruments and regimes I work across complementary facilities: VLT/CRIRES+ ($R\sim 10^{5}$) — Workhorse for the ESO SupJup Survey and for β Pic b. The K-band CO overtone region near 2.3 μm is particularly powerful for carbon isotopes. JWST/NIRSpec ($R\sim 2700$) — Broad 1–5 μm coverage reaches the CO fundamental band near 4.6 μm, enabling simultaneous atmospheric and disc constraints that are difficult from the ground. SPIRou / CFHT (archival) — High-S/N K-band spectra of nearby M dwarfs for Galactic chemical evolution studies. My contribution Built and applied Bayesian atmospheric retrievals coupling petitRADTRANS with nested sampling (e.g. MultiNest / UltraNest) to forward-model observed spectra. Led multi-epoch CRIRES+ programmes where night-by-night retrievals are combined so that systematic epoch scatter enters the final error budget (β Pic b). For close-in companions, developed extraction strategies that weight spatial rows by cross-correlation strength after modelling residual starlight — critical when the planet sits on a bright slit...

title: Isotope Ratios
content: ← All research topics Isotope ratios Beyond bulk elemental abundances, isotopic ratios record nucleosynthesis, disc chemistry, and the balance of gas versus solid accretion. Carbon ($^{12}\mathrm{C}/^{13}\mathrm{C}$) and oxygen ($^{16}\mathrm{O}/^{18}\mathrm{O}$) are especially accessible in cool atmospheres through CO and H$_2$O isotopologues. Why isotopes? In protoplanetary discs, ion-exchange reactions and isotope-selective photodissociation can fractionate $^{12}\mathrm{C}/^{13}\mathrm{C}$ between gas and ice, so a planet’s atmospheric ratio may depend on birth location relative to snow lines. In the Galaxy, $^{12}\mathrm{C}$ and $^{16}\mathrm{O}$ are primary products of helium burning, while $^{13}\mathrm{C}$ is largely a secondary CNO-cycle product. Trends of isotope ratios with metallicity therefore test Galactic chemical evolution (GCE) models — including the role of novae as $^{13}\mathrm{C}$ sources. My contribution Planets and brown dwarfs (ESO SupJup and follow-ups) Measured $^{12}\mathrm{C}/^{13}\mathrm{C}$ in young brown dwarfs with CRIRES+, including TWA 28 ($81^{+28}{-19}$) and J0856 ($79^{+20}{-14}$), consistent with the local ISM and favouring fragmentation-like formation (SupJup II). Extended this programme to GQ Lup B and its host star (SupJup IV) and to the directly imaged planet β Pic b ($58^{+18}_{-15}$; A&A 2026). With JWST/NIRSpec, constrained both carbon and oxygen isotopes in TWA 27A and TWA 28 from the CO fundamental and water isotopologues (A&A 2025). Cool stars Led...

title: M Dwarfs
content: ← All research topics M dwarfs M dwarfs make up roughly three-quarters of stars in the Milky Way. They are long-lived, chemically relatively pristine after formation, and their cool atmospheres are rich in molecular lines — including the CO features needed to measure rare carbon and oxygen isotopes. Scientific motivation Elemental abundances alone leave degeneracies in Galactic chemical evolution. Isotope ratios add orthogonal constraints because different isotopes form through distinct channels: primary helium burning versus secondary CNO processing (and, for $^{18}\mathrm{O}$, metallicity- and rotation-dependent yields in massive stars). Until recently, precise $^{12}\mathrm{C}/^{13}\mathrm{C}$ and $^{16}\mathrm{O}/^{18}\mathrm{O}$ measurements in M dwarfs were scarce. My contribution In González Picos, Snellen & de Regt (2025, Nature Astronomy) we analysed archival SPIRou K-band spectra of 32 nearby M dwarfs (within ~15 pc), spanning [M/H] from about −0.4 to +0.4: $^{13}\mathrm{CO}$ was detected at $>3\sigma$ in 29/32 stars; $\mathrm{C}^{18}\mathrm{O}$ in a subset, with upper limits elsewhere. We find a clear trend of decreasing $^{12}\mathrm{C}/^{13}\mathrm{C}$ with increasing metallicity, consistent with GCE models in which novae enrich the ISM in $^{13}\mathrm{C}$ over the past few Gyr. Super-solar metallicity stars approach present-day ISM-like carbon isotope ratios (~68), while $^{16}\mathrm{O}/^{18}\mathrm{O}$ in the most metal-rich objects can fall well below solar values....
